Early signal•Peer-reviewed retrospective development and independent hold-out validation study•September 27, 2026

Local LLM reaches expert-level lecanemab pre-screen accuracy

In a 99-record independent hold-out set, an on-premises language-model pipeline classified lecanemab eligibility with 93.9% accuracy and κ 0.903, outperforming a deterministic rule-based extractor (79.8% accuracy; p=0.0026), but it remains an uncertified single-center retrospective triage tool requiring clinician review.

Key quantitative results: In the 99-record hold-out set, consensus classified 16 as eligible, 43 as potentially eligible and 40 as not eligible. The LLM pipeline achieved 93.9% accuracy (95% CI 88.9% to 98.0%) and κ 0.903 (95% CI 0.810 to 0.968), with six disagreements.

ManagementDisease-modifying treatment eligibility

Added September 28, 2026 · DOI:10.1002/dad2.70495; PMID:42802831

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The privacy-preserving pipeline could reduce chart-review burden and flag missing amyloid, MRI or cognitive data without sending protected health information to an external cloud. Its hold-out performance was comparable to two expert raters, but six errors included medication/disease categorization, context interpretation and threshold application. Prospective multicenter validation is needed before operational deployment.

Study design

The investigators used 97 German memory-clinic consultation reports to optimize prompts, a deterministic comparator and a shared three-class eligibility rule set, then locked the systems before evaluating 99 temporally and patient-wise distinct hold-out reports. Two clinicians independently classified the hold-out set as eligible, potentially eligible or not eligible, with consensus as the reference standard.

Key quantitative results

  • In the 99-record hold-out set, consensus classified 16 as eligible, 43 as potentially eligible and 40 as not eligible. The LLM pipeline achieved 93.9% accuracy (95% CI 88.9% to 98.0%) and κ 0.903 (95% CI 0.810 to 0.968), with six disagreements.
  • For case finding after combining eligible and potentially eligible, sensitivity was 91.5% (95% CI 83.1% to 98.3%) and specificity 97.5% (95% CI 91.1% to 100.0%); PPV was 98%. Eligible-class sensitivity was 100%.
  • The deterministic extractor achieved 79.8% accuracy and κ 0.673. The paired accuracy difference was 14.1 percentage points (95% CI 6.1 to 22.2; McNemar p=0.0026), while individual experts achieved 91.9% and 93.9% accuracy.

What changed

A September 27 publication now provides locked hold-out performance for a locally deployed language model intended to support lecanemab eligibility pre-screening while keeping patient records on premises.

Strength of evidence

Promising but early implementation evidence with strict separation of development and hold-out sets, a consensus reference and paired comparator. Generalizability is limited by retrospective single-center German documentation, only 99 validation records, local AUR-derived rules, missing APOE information and no prospective workflow, patient-safety or access outcome.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

The system may help triage charts and identify missing workup elements, but it should not determine eligibility or replace clinician review. Eligibility remains governed by the applicable label, clinical evaluation, amyloid confirmation, MRI findings, comorbidities, concomitant medications and shared decision-making.

Field medical relevance

Relevant to operational scaling of disease-modifying therapy programs, protected-data handling, chart abstraction and consistency of eligibility review. It is management workflow research, not biomarker-validation evidence.

Quanterix or platform relevance

The model extracted eligibility-relevant facts from German narrative memory-clinic reports and fed them to a shared rule-based classifier. Performance depends on local documentation, operationalized criteria and human oversight; the model was not tested as an autonomous decision-maker.

Access or reimbursement relevance

The on-premises design addresses data-protection barriers and may improve screening capacity, but no commercial availability, medical-device authorization, reimbursement or coverage was established.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Was the model tested prospectively in routine care?
No. The study retrospectively classified narrative reports; it did not measure clinician time, missed contraindications in live use, treatment access, safety or patient outcomes.
Why is this not tagged Biomarkers?
Its central question was automated treatment-eligibility triage. Amyloid and MRI information were input variables, not the object of biomarker measurement, validity or interpretation research.
Can the model make treatment decisions?
No. It is an uncertified triage support system, made six hold-out errors and cannot infer facts absent from the record; the authors call for clinician supervision and prospective validation.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Retrospective single-center study using German consultation reports
  • Small 99-record independent validation set with only 16 fully eligible cases
  • Local AUR-derived rules may not match labels or policies in other jurisdictions
  • APOE genotype was missing and source documentation predated routine anti-amyloid implementation
  • Six validation errors included medication, disease, context and threshold interpretation
  • No prospective time-saving, decision-impact, safety, access or patient-outcome evaluation

Primary source · DOI · PubMed record · Free full text

Miklitz C, Shrestha M, Philipp W, et al. Locally deployed large language model for real-world lecanemab eligibility pre-screening. Alzheimers Dement (Amst). 2026;18(3):e70495. doi:10.1002/dad2.70495.

Implementation-relevant•Peer-reviewed real-world diagnostic-accuracy cohort•September 24, 2026

Standalone LUMIPULSE p-tau217 exceeds 90/90 in treatment candidates

In 99 Japanese patients undergoing anti-amyloid-treatment screening, standalone LUMIPULSE plasma p-tau217 identified PET- or CSF-confirmed amyloid positivity with AUC 0.93, 95.1% sensitivity and 94.1% specificity at a cohort-derived 0.1795 pg/mL cutpoint, but the 80.0% negative predictive value and threshold instability argue against using a negative result alone to exclude treatment candidacy.

Key quantitative results: Amyloid positivity was confirmed in 82/99 (82.8%). Plasma p-tau217 achieved AUC 0.93 (95% CI 0.82 to 1.00); at 0.1795 pg/mL there were 78 true positives, 16 true negatives, one false positive and four false negatives, yielding 95.1% sensitivity, 94.1% specificity, 98.7% PPV and 80.0% NPV.

BiomarkersBloodp-tau217AmyloidBiological confirmation

Added September 28, 2026 · DOI:10.1002/dad2.70497; PMID:42787809

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The cohort addresses the exact high-prevalence population in which blood tests may be used to streamline confirmatory testing before anti-amyloid therapy. Performance met the Alzheimer’s Association 90% sensitivity/specificity benchmark at an internally selected threshold, but only 17 patients were amyloid-negative, three of four false negatives were below the assay detection limit, and external higher cutpoints reduced NPV to 55.2%. This is clinical-validity and workflow evidence, not analytical validation or proof that blood-first triage improves outcomes.

Study design

Investigators studied 99 patients evaluated for amyloid-targeting treatment at one Japanese specialty clinic from January through October 2024: 62 had MCI and 37 mild dementia. Amyloid status was confirmed by approved CSF Aβ42/Aβ40 testing in 49 or amyloid PET in 50. Stored plasma was batch-tested for p-tau217 on LUMIPULSE G1200; diagnostic performance was assessed against the PET/CSF reference standard, with the main cutpoint selected in the same cohort by the Youden index.

Key quantitative results

  • Amyloid positivity was confirmed in 82/99 (82.8%). Plasma p-tau217 achieved AUC 0.93 (95% CI 0.82 to 1.00); at 0.1795 pg/mL there were 78 true positives, 16 true negatives, one false positive and four false negatives, yielding 95.1% sensitivity, 94.1% specificity, 98.7% PPV and 80.0% NPV.
  • Three external LUMIPULSE p-tau217 cutpoints from 0.212 to 0.247 pg/mL preserved 94.1% specificity and PPV above 98% but lowered sensitivity to 84.1%–90.2% and NPV as low as 55.2%.
  • A two-cutpoint strategy using 0.1465 pg/mL for negativity and 0.1795 pg/mL for positivity classified 5.1% as intermediate and produced 97.5% sensitivity, 92.9% specificity, 98.7% PPV and 86.7% NPV; the authors still advised confirmatory testing after a negative result when pretest probability is high.

What changed

A newly indexed, source-date September 24 study provides real-world performance data for standalone automated p-tau217 specifically among patients already screened as potential candidates for amyloid-targeting treatment.

Strength of evidence

Moderate clinical-validity evidence from a clinically relevant cohort with PET or approved CSF reference testing. Confidence is limited by the single-center retrospective design, only 17 amyloid-negative participants, selection and biobank-enrollment bias, batch testing, internally optimized threshold and no independent validation cohort.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

A positive result was highly predictive in this enriched cohort, but negative results were not sufficiently reliable to rule out amyloid pathology. The data support locally validated triage workflows and prevalence-aware interpretation, not substitution of this standalone research cutpoint for labeled assays or confirmatory testing without further validation.

Field medical relevance

Directly relevant to blood-based biomarker implementation, anti-amyloid treatment workup, threshold transferability and communication about why PPV/NPV change with population prevalence.

Quanterix or platform relevance

Stored plasma was batch-tested on the LUMIPULSE G1200. The study evaluated standalone p-tau217 with a locally optimized cutpoint, not the FDA-cleared LUMIPULSE pTau217/Aβ42 plasma ratio and not routine on-demand analytical performance.

Access or reimbursement relevance

The report establishes no new authorization, commercial availability, guideline endorsement, coverage or reimbursement. Standalone LUMIPULSE plasma p-tau217 was described by the manufacturer as research use only in the United States; the FDA-cleared Fujirebio plasma product is the pTau217/Aβ42 ratio.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Did the study validate the FDA-cleared LUMIPULSE plasma ratio?
No. It evaluated standalone plasma p-tau217 on the LUMIPULSE platform. The US-cleared Fujirebio test uses the pTau217/Aβ42 ratio with its labeled interpretation.
Can a negative result rule out amyloid pathology before treatment?
Not reliably in this high-prevalence cohort. NPV was 80.0% at the optimized single cutpoint and 86.7% with two cutpoints; the authors advised confirmatory testing when clinical suspicion remains high.
Was clinical utility proven?
No. The study measured diagnostic classification in stored samples; it did not test whether a blood-first strategy changes treatment decisions, time to care, cost, safety or patient outcomes.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Single specialty center in Japan with only 99 participants and 17 amyloid-negative cases
  • Very high amyloid prevalence and biobank-enrollment bias inflate PPV and constrain NPV precision
  • Primary threshold selected and evaluated in the same cohort without external validation
  • Batch testing of stored plasma may understate routine on-demand variability
  • Mixed PET and CSF reference standards and incomplete APOE data
  • No analytical-validation, decision-impact, health-economic or patient-outcome endpoint

Primary source · DOI · PubMed record · Free full text

Shimasaki R, Kurihara M, Sato K, et al. Clinical utility of LUMIPULSE plasma p-tau217 to identify amyloid positivity among candidates for amyloid-targeting treatments in a real-world cohort. Alzheimers Dement (Amst). 2026;18(3):e70497. doi:10.1002/dad2.70497.

Practice-relevant•Peer-reviewed retrospective real-world treatment cohort•September 24, 2026

Japanese lecanemab cohort quantifies screening and early ARIA

Of 321 patients screened at one Japanese memory clinic, 102 started lecanemab; among 70 with serial MRI surveillance, 8 (11.4%) developed ARIA within six months, while infusion reactions occurred in 28/102 (27.5%) and 13/102 (12.7%) discontinued treatment.

Key quantitative results: Treatment started in 102/321 (31.8%). Before amyloid testing, 154/320 (48.1%) were excluded or deferred after MRI/cognitive assessment; 54/165 (32.5%) who underwent amyloid PET were negative, and 13/102 (12.7%) treated patients discontinued within six months.

ManagementMRIDisease-modifying treatment eligibility

Added September 28, 2026 · DOI:10.1002/dad2.70492; PMID:42798750

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

This cohort exposes the operational funnel around lecanemab: only 31.8% of clinically suspected patients initiated treatment after cognition, MRI, amyloid confirmation and preference were considered. Early safety was broadly manageable under structured MRI surveillance, but four ARIA cases led to discontinuation and nearly one in eight treated patients stopped for clinical, logistical or financial reasons. The uncontrolled six-month cognitive data cannot establish effectiveness.

Study design

A Japanese memory clinic retrospectively followed 321 people with suspected MCI due to Alzheimer disease or mild Alzheimer dementia considered for lecanemab. MRI and structured cognitive testing preceded amyloid confirmation; 102 patients received at least one infusion. Safety and continuity analyses included all treated patients, ARIA incidence used the 70 who had serial MRI surveillance within six months, and paired cognitive analyses included 66 six-month completers.

Key quantitative results

  • Treatment started in 102/321 (31.8%). Before amyloid testing, 154/320 (48.1%) were excluded or deferred after MRI/cognitive assessment; 54/165 (32.5%) who underwent amyloid PET were negative, and 13/102 (12.7%) treated patients discontinued within six months.
  • ARIA occurred in 8/70 (11.4%) patients with serial MRI: isolated ARIA-H in 10.0% and combined ARIA-E+H in 1.4%, with no isolated ARIA-E. One macrohemorrhage and two moderate-to-severe ARIA-H cases led to discontinuation; a fourth mild ARIA-H case stopped because of advanced age.
  • Infusion reactions occurred in 28/102 (27.5%), most commonly fever (14.7%); 2/102 (2.0%) discontinued for persistent reactions. Among 66 six-month completers, MMSE fell from 25.0 to 23.9 (p=0.005) and CDR-SB rose from 1.56 to 1.77 (p=0.026), without an untreated comparator.

What changed

A newly indexed, source-date September 24 cohort provides a complete real-world screening funnel plus structured six-month ARIA, infusion-reaction, persistence and discontinuation data from routine Japanese practice.

Strength of evidence

Moderate implementation and safety evidence from a well-described real-world cohort with structured MRI surveillance. The single-center retrospective design, changing denominators, short follow-up, mild treated population and absence of a control group prevent causal efficacy comparisons or precise risk estimates for broader practice.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

The study reinforces the need to plan MRI capacity, infusion-reaction management and counseling about treatment burden before initiation. Its ARIA estimates should not replace label-based monitoring or individualized risk assessment, and the six-month cognitive changes should not be interpreted as proof of benefit or failure.

Field medical relevance

Directly relevant to disease-modifying treatment eligibility, operational access, ARIA surveillance, APOE discussions, infusion management and persistence in routine care.

Access or reimbursement relevance

Lecanemab was covered by Japanese national insurance, but copayments of 10%–30%, frequent infusions and travel affected uptake or persistence. The study documents access friction; it does not establish a new coverage or reimbursement policy.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
How many screened patients actually started lecanemab?
102 of 321 (31.8%). Cognitive stage, MRI safety findings, amyloid negativity, patient preference and logistical or financial concerns all narrowed the funnel.
Was the ARIA rate 11.4% of all 102 treated patients?
No. The numerator was eight and the denominator was 70 patients with serial MRI surveillance within six months. The publication used changing denominators as patients reached follow-up milestones.
Did stable six-month cognition demonstrate effectiveness?
No. Only 66 completers had paired measures, MMSE and CDR-SB worsened modestly, and there was no untreated comparator.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Retrospective single-center cohort with modest treated sample
  • ARIA estimate based on 70 serially monitored patients rather than all 102 treated patients
  • Only six months of follow-up and predominantly CDR 0.5 disease
  • No untreated or matched comparator for cognitive outcomes
  • Selection, treatment-preference and attrition effects limit generalizability
  • Japanese eligibility, reimbursement and MRI practice may differ from other jurisdictions

Primary source · DOI · PubMed record · Free full text

Shimohama S, Bun S, Shikimoto R, et al. Real-world implementation of lecanemab in Alzheimer's disease: A Japanese cohort. Alzheimers Dement (Amst). 2026;18(3):e70492. doi:10.1002/dad2.70492.

Implementation-relevant•Peer-reviewed consecutive real-world memory-clinic biomarker cohort•September 23, 2026

Real-world amyloid PET yield rises across the clinical continuum

In 194 consecutive memory-clinic patients, amyloid PET positivity rose from 40.9% in subjective cognitive decline to 66.0% in MCI and 91.7% in early Alzheimer disease, while MRI/VSRAD indices added essentially no discrimination beyond clinical diagnosis (cross-validated AUC 0.752 versus 0.751).

Key quantitative results: Amyloid PET positivity increased stepwise from 38/93 (40.9%) in subjective cognitive decline to 31/47 (66.0%) in MCI and 50/54 (91.7%) in early Alzheimer disease (p<0.0001).

BiomarkersAmyloid PETAmyloidBiological confirmation

Added September 24, 2026 · DOI:10.1177/13872877261490596; PMID:42775784

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The consecutive-clinic design gives useful real-world context for pretest probability and shows that commonly used structural MRI indices did not add amyloid-status discrimination. It supports clinical validity of amyloid PET in the studied setting, not analytical validation or clinical utility: no management-change or outcome endpoint was tested, and positivity in subjective cognitive decline should not be equated with a clinical Alzheimer diagnosis.

Study design

The investigators retrospectively analyzed 194 consecutive patients who underwent florbetapir PET in one memory-clinic setting: 93 with subjective cognitive decline, 47 with MCI and 54 with early Alzheimer disease. Certified visual reads defined positivity; continuous Centiloid and regional SUVR measures quantified burden. MRI/VSRAD indices were available for 153 patients, and models were compared with cross-validated AUC.

Key quantitative results

  • Amyloid PET positivity increased stepwise from 38/93 (40.9%) in subjective cognitive decline to 31/47 (66.0%) in MCI and 50/54 (91.7%) in early Alzheimer disease (p<0.0001).
  • Centiloid values and regional SUVRs increased in parallel across the groups, with the largest regional differences in the temporal cortex and precuneus.
  • Adding MRI/VSRAD indices to the base clinical model did not improve cross-validated discrimination of amyloid positivity: AUC 0.752 with MRI versus 0.751 without it.

What changed

A source-date-new consecutive memory-clinic study now quantifies amyloid PET positivity across subjective cognitive decline, MCI and early Alzheimer disease and directly tests the incremental value of routinely used MRI/VSRAD indices.

Strength of evidence

Moderate real-world clinical-validity evidence from a consecutive cohort with certified reads and cross-validation. The single-center retrospective design, clinically assigned groups, incomplete MRI data and absence of a decision-impact or patient-outcome endpoint limit implementation claims.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

The observed gradient can inform pretest-probability discussions, and the near-identical AUCs argue against assuming that VSRAD meaningfully predicts amyloid status beyond clinical classification. PET results still require interpretation in the full clinical context and according to the tracer label.

Field medical relevance

Directly relevant to amyloid-confirmation pathways, DMT workup discussions and the distinction between structural neurodegeneration markers and amyloid pathology. It also illustrates why a positive scan is not itself a stand-alone clinical diagnosis.

Quanterix or platform relevance

Amyloid status was assigned by certified visual reads and quantified with Centiloids and regional SUVRs. VSRAD MRI indices correlated with amyloid burden but did not improve cross-validated discrimination beyond the clinical group model.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No new authorization, tracer availability, guideline endorsement, coverage or reimbursement change follows from this report.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Does 40.9% positivity in subjective cognitive decline support screening asymptomatic people?
No. This was a referred memory-clinic cohort, not a population-screening sample, and the study did not test benefits, harms or outcomes from screening.
Did MRI add useful prediction of amyloid positivity?
Not in the cross-validated models: the AUC changed from 0.751 to 0.752 after VSRAD indices were added.
Was clinical utility established?
No. The study measured biomarker prevalence and discrimination; it did not test whether PET-guided decisions changed management or improved outcomes.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Single-center retrospective cohort with a modest sample
  • Memory-clinic referral population limits generalizability and cannot estimate population screening yield
  • MRI/VSRAD data were available for 153 of 194 participants
  • Clinical categories were not an independent neuropathology reference standard
  • No management-change, decision-impact, cost-effectiveness or patient-outcome endpoint

Primary source · DOI · PubMed record

Arai H, Aiba S, Yamamoto H, Akiba Y, Takayama J, Arai R. Clinic-based real-world analysis of amyloid PET positivity and MRI markers across subjective cognitive decline, mild cognitive impairment, and early Alzheimer's disease. J Alzheimers Dis. Published online September 23, 2026. doi:10.1177/13872877261490596.

Important new evidence•Peer-reviewed randomized placebo-controlled biomarker analysis•September 23, 2026

COSMOS finds no multivitamin or cocoa effect on blood biomarkers

In a randomized COSMOS ancillary study with 498 to 506 participants, neither a daily multivitamin nor cocoa extract changed two-year trajectories of plasma N-terminal tau, neurofilament light or oligomeric amyloid-beta; every treatment-versus-placebo comparison was nonsignificant.

Key quantitative results: Multivitamin versus placebo produced no significant difference in yearly change for NT1 (3.7%, 95% CI -3.0% to 10.8%; p=0.29), NfL (3.1%, -1.9% to 8.3%; p=0.23) or oligomeric amyloid-beta (-8.9%, -23.9% to 9.0%; p=0.31).

BiomarkersClinical TrialsBloodNeurofilament lightN-terminal tau fragmentPharmacodynamic research

Added September 24, 2026 · NCT02422745; DOI:10.1177/13872877261489739; PMID:42775737

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The randomized design makes this a cleaner mechanistic test than observational supplement studies. The uniformly null biomarker results weaken claims that the tested multivitamin or cocoa extract affects these blood-marker trajectories over two years, but they do not negate previously reported cognitive findings because NT1, NfL and oligomeric amyloid-beta are not validated surrogate endpoints for prevention benefit.

Study design

COSMOS randomized older US adults in a 2-by-2 factorial design to a daily multivitamin-mineral supplement, cocoa extract containing 500 mg/day of flavanols including 80 mg of epicatechin, both interventions or matching placebos. This ancillary analysis included 506 participants with NT1 or NfL measurements and 498 with oligomeric amyloid-beta measurements and modeled yearly percentage change over two years.

Key quantitative results

  • Multivitamin versus placebo produced no significant difference in yearly change for NT1 (3.7%, 95% CI -3.0% to 10.8%; p=0.29), NfL (3.1%, -1.9% to 8.3%; p=0.23) or oligomeric amyloid-beta (-8.9%, -23.9% to 9.0%; p=0.31).
  • Cocoa extract versus placebo also produced no significant difference for NT1 (-0.7%, 95% CI -7.1% to 6.1%; p=0.83), NfL (0.5%, -4.4% to 5.6%; p=0.85) or oligomeric amyloid-beta (-5.9%, -21.4% to 12.6%; p=0.51).
  • The analysis included 506 participants for NT1/NfL and 498 for oligomeric amyloid-beta; the biomarker outcomes were measured over two years.

What changed

A new randomized analysis now directly tests whether the COSMOS multivitamin and cocoa interventions alter three blood-biomarker trajectories and finds no detectable effect for either intervention.

Strength of evidence

Moderate randomized mechanistic evidence with placebo controls and repeated biomarker measurements. It is an ancillary subset, the confidence intervals permit modest effects, the measures are not validated surrogate endpoints and the abstract does not establish analytical-performance characteristics for the assays.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

The findings do not support using these biomarkers to claim a biological response to the tested supplements or using the supplements to modify these biomarker trajectories. They do not establish absence of cognitive benefit or harm and should not be converted into an Alzheimer treatment recommendation.

Field medical relevance

Relevant to prevention-trial interpretation, pharmacodynamic claims and communication about supplement mechanisms. It separates a null randomized biomarker effect from analytical validity, clinical utility and clinical outcomes.

Quanterix or platform relevance

The report evaluated within-person change in three exploratory neurodegeneration-related blood measures. It did not validate them as surrogate endpoints, establish clinical cutoffs or show that changes predict cognitive benefit.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No assay authorization, availability, guideline endorsement, coverage or reimbursement change follows from the report.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Does this prove multivitamins or cocoa have no cognitive effect?
No. It shows no detectable effect on the three measured blood biomarkers over two years; those biomarkers are not validated surrogates for cognitive outcomes.
Are these biomarkers authorized for monitoring supplement response?
No. The paper does not establish an authorized or guideline-endorsed monitoring use.
Why is this both Biomarkers and Clinical Trials?
The primary analysis is a prospective randomized intervention comparison, and its central outcomes are changes in blood biomarkers; both topics independently describe the report's main purpose.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Ancillary subset rather than the full COSMOS randomized population
  • No validated surrogate relationship between these biomarker changes and cognitive benefit
  • Confidence intervals do not exclude modest positive or negative effects
  • Population was older US adults selected for the parent cardiovascular and cancer-prevention trial, not biomarker-confirmed Alzheimer disease
  • No new analytical-validation, cutoff, decision-impact or clinical-utility evidence

Primary source · DOI · Journal abstract · ClinicalTrials.gov record

Rist PM, Li S, Hamaya R, et al. Effect of a multivitamin and cocoa flavanol extract on changes in neurofilament light, N-terminal tau fragment, and oligomeric amyloid-beta levels in COSMOS-clinic. J Alzheimers Dis. Published online September 23, 2026. doi:10.1177/13872877261489739.

Practice-relevant•Peer-reviewed population-wide matched observational cohort•September 23, 2026

Dementia risk remains elevated for years after TIA

Among 113,081 matched patients with a first TIA, 19.3% developed dementia over mean 7.11-year follow-up; risk was highest in year one (HR 1.75) and remained elevated overall (HR 1.34), supporting long-term cognitive surveillance alongside vascular prevention.

Key quantitative results: Dementia was diagnosed in 19.3% of 113,081 matched patients with TIA over mean follow-up of 7.11 years (SD 5.16). The dementia rate was 2.71 versus 2.03 per 100 person-years in matched controls.

ManagementDementia-risk counseling

Added September 24, 2026 · DOI:10.1212/WNL.0000000000218554; PMID:42777184

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The scale and long follow-up show that cognitive risk after TIA is not confined to the early post-event period or explained solely by subsequent stroke. The study supports sustained attention to cognition and vascular prevention, but administrative dementia ascertainment cannot determine Alzheimer versus vascular etiology, and the observational design does not prove that a specific screening schedule or intervention prevents dementia.

Study design

Ontario administrative data identified adults with a first emergency-department visit or admission for TIA from 2002 through 2022. After excluding prior dementia, prior stroke, early death and long-term-care admission, 113,081 patients were matched to population controls on age, sex, deprivation, rurality and vascular comorbidities and separately matched to patients with first stroke. Follow-up began 90 days after the index event; dementia was identified with a validated claims-and-medication algorithm.

Key quantitative results

  • Dementia was diagnosed in 19.3% of 113,081 matched patients with TIA over mean follow-up of 7.11 years (SD 5.16). The dementia rate was 2.71 versus 2.03 per 100 person-years in matched controls.
  • Compared with controls, dementia risk was highest within the first year (HR 1.75, 95% CI 1.66 to 1.85) and remained elevated over the full follow-up (overall HR 1.34, 95% CI 1.31 to 1.36), which extended to 20 years.
  • Compared with first stroke, dementia hazard after TIA was lower at one year (HR 0.67, 95% CI 0.64 to 0.70) but converged by five years; adjustment for incident stroke only minimally attenuated the TIA association.

What changed

A population-wide study now quantifies the time course of dementia after TIA against both matched community controls and stroke, showing a persistent excess extending well beyond the period of acute stroke prevention.

Strength of evidence

Strong association evidence from a very large matched population cohort with competing-risk and time-varying analyses. Residual confounding, claims-based exposure and outcome ascertainment, lack of dementia-subtype adjudication and survivorship selection preclude causal or Alzheimer-specific conclusions.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

TIA should be treated as a marker of sustained cognitive risk as well as recurrent vascular risk. The evidence supports counseling, attention to cognitive change and aggressive evidence-based vascular prevention, but it does not establish an optimal screening interval or a dementia-preventive effect of any specific intervention.

Field medical relevance

Relevant to risk-reduction and general-management discussions, especially the interface of vascular events and later dementia. It should not be presented as biomarker research or as evidence of Alzheimer-specific causation.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No new authorization, guideline endorsement, coverage or reimbursement change follows from this report.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Was the excess dementia risk explained by later stroke?
Only minimally. Adjustment for incident stroke had little effect, although residual vascular and health-system confounding remains possible.
Does the study identify Alzheimer disease specifically?
No. Dementia was ascertained from administrative diagnoses, claims and dementia medications without subtype adjudication or biomarker confirmation.
Does it prescribe a cognitive-screening schedule?
No. It supports long-term vigilance but did not test screening intervals, decision impact or whether screening changes outcomes.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Observational administrative-data design with possible residual confounding and exposure misclassification
  • Claims-and-medication dementia algorithm without subtype or Alzheimer biomarker adjudication
  • Exclusion of early deaths and long-term-care admissions limits applicability to the sickest patients
  • No direct cognitive testing or functional trajectory
  • No intervention, screening-schedule or clinical-utility evaluation

Primary source · DOI · PubMed record

Joundi RA, Fang J, Austin PC, et al. Long-Term Risk of Dementia After TIA: A Population-Wide Matched Cohort Study. Neurology. 2026;107(8):e218554. doi:10.1212/WNL.0000000000218554.

Implementation-relevant•Peer-reviewed prospective multicenter cross-sectional validation study•September 21, 2026

Five-class tau PET framework detects more early pathology

In 681 participants, a five-class visual framework achieved interrater kappa values of 0.77 to 0.85 and classified more cognitively unimpaired and MCI participants as tau-positive than the FDA-approved flortaucipir binary read, but the new framework itself is not authorized or guideline-endorsed and has no proven clinical utility.

Key quantitative results: Interrater agreement for the five classes was kappa 0.77 to 0.85. Intertracer agreement was highest for MK-6240 versus flortaucipir (kappa 0.88); across all tracer pairs, five-class percentage agreement ranged from 75.2% to 83.3%.

BiomarkersTau PETTau tanglesAmyloidTau pathology staging

Added September 22, 2026 · DOI:10.1001/jamaneurol.2026.3253; PMID:42766299

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The harmonized approach moves tau PET beyond a late-stage binary read and provides a common vocabulary across four tracers. It increases early-stage positivity and tracks with cognition and other biomarkers, but the same cohort was used to develop and evaluate it, and no prospective decision-impact or outcome study has established clinical utility.

Study design

The HEAD study enrolled adults aged 50 to 90 years at nine North American and European sites. The analysis included 681 participants (369 cognitively unimpaired, 245 with MCI and 67 with dementia) who underwent two to four tau PET scans, amyloid PET, MRI and cognitive assessment. Blinded readers assigned negative, low, moderate, high or atypical classes from seven composite regions.

Key quantitative results

  • Interrater agreement for the five classes was kappa 0.77 to 0.85. Intertracer agreement was highest for MK-6240 versus flortaucipir (kappa 0.88); across all tracer pairs, five-class percentage agreement ranged from 75.2% to 83.3%.
  • Among cognitively unimpaired participants, the FDA-approved flortaucipir binary read was positive in 26/364, versus 49/364 with harmonized flortaucipir (prevalence ratio 1.89, 95% CI 1.31 to 2.70) and 71/364 with harmonized MK-6240 (2.73, 1.95 to 3.83). In MCI, the corresponding counts were 100/223, 123/223 (1.23, 1.12 to 1.35) and 142/223 (1.42, 1.27 to 1.59).
  • From low to high tau classes, cognition was 1.4-fold worse, amyloid PET burden 3.2-fold higher and plasma p-tau217 2.5-fold higher; positivity estimates converged in dementia at 45/57, 47/57 and 50/57 for the regulatory, harmonized flortaucipir and harmonized MK-6240 reads.

What changed

A peer-reviewed prospective multicenter study now provides a reproducible five-class visual staging framework across four tau PET tracers and quantifies how much more early-stage pathology it detects than the approved flortaucipir binary read.

Strength of evidence

Strong agreement and convergent clinical-validity evidence within a large head-to-head imaging cohort. Analytical validity and reader reproducibility were not established outside the study, the framework was developed and evaluated in the same cohort, and longitudinal prognostic and decision-impact validation are still needed.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

The framework may improve research staging and trial enrichment, especially before dementia, but it should not be substituted for an approved tracer's labeled read or used alone for treatment decisions until externally validated and implemented under appropriate guidance.

Field medical relevance

Directly relevant to imaging interpretation, biological staging and blood-biomarker studies that use tau PET as a reference. It also shows that tracer and reading method can change apparent positivity in early disease.

Quanterix or platform relevance

The method uses tracer-specific images but a common seven-region, five-class visual scheme. Agreement was strongest for MK-6240 and flortaucipir, and performance was lower for some regions with PI-2620, so tracer equivalence should not be assumed.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No new authorization, commercial availability, guideline endorsement, coverage or reimbursement follows from the framework. A free research visual-reading tool is available, but access to tracers, scanners and trained readers remains separate.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Is this five-class read FDA approved?
No. Tauvid and Tauklarify are approved tracers with their own labeled visual-read methods; this harmonized framework is a research method and has no separate authorization.
Does greater positivity prove better diagnosis or outcomes?
No. The study supports agreement and association with disease measures, but it did not establish that the additional early positives improve decisions, outcomes or treatment selection.
Can results be treated as interchangeable across tracers?
No. Agreement was good to excellent overall but varied by tracer and region, and atypical classifications did not converge across tracers.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Framework development and evaluation occurred in the same cohort without external validation
  • Cross-sectional design without longitudinal prognostic or treatment-response assessment
  • Smaller RO948 and PI-2620 samples and lower regional confidence for PI-2620
  • Predominantly highly educated White non-Hispanic academic-research cohort
  • No neuropathology reference standard, decision-impact study or clinical-utility evaluation

Primary source · DOI · JAMA Neurology full text · Research visual-reading tool

Benedet AL, et al; HEAD study. A Harmonized Visual Reading Framework for Tau PET Staging in Alzheimer Disease. JAMA Neurol. Published online September 21, 2026. doi:10.1001/jamaneurol.2026.3253.

Important new evidence•Peer-reviewed multicohort observational biomarker analysis•September 21, 2026

GFAP further stratifies decline among p-tau217-positive adults

Across 3,505 participants from six cohorts, co-elevated plasma GFAP and p-tau217 was associated with 62% faster annual CDR-SB progression and a 28% higher hazard of clinical worsening than p-tau217 positivity alone, supporting prognostic enrichment but not clinical utility.

Key quantitative results: Compared with p-tau217-positive/GFAP-negative participants, those positive for both biomarkers had a 62% faster annual CDR-SB progression rate (p=0.008).

BiomarkersBloodPlasma GFAPPlasma p-tau217Prognostic stratification

Added September 22, 2026 · DOI:10.1186/s13024-026-00995-5

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The study asks a clinically useful biomarker question: why people with elevated p-tau217 can follow different courses. GFAP added prognostic separation across multiple cohorts, but the association is observational, GFAP is nonspecific, thresholds were cohort-specific and the hazard ratio was modest with a lower confidence bound near 1.

Study design

Pooled analysis of 3,505 individuals across six independent cohorts spanning cognitively unimpaired aging through Alzheimer disease. All had baseline amyloid PET, plasma GFAP, plasma p-tau217 and CDR-SB. Four biomarker groups were followed for up to five years; models assessed baseline severity, annual CDR-SB change and time to a CDR-SB increase of at least 0.5 points.

Key quantitative results

  • Compared with p-tau217-positive/GFAP-negative participants, those positive for both biomarkers had a 62% faster annual CDR-SB progression rate (p=0.008).
  • Dual-positive participants had a higher hazard of clinical worsening, defined as a CDR-SB increase of at least 0.5 points (hazard ratio 1.28, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.61).
  • The GFAP-by-p-tau217 interaction accounted for 68.6% of biomarker-attributable variance in individual annual CDR-SB change, compared with 25.3% for p-tau217 and 1.1% for GFAP independent effects.

What changed

A large multicohort longitudinal analysis now quantifies how astrocyte-reactivity status may separate progression risk within the clinically heterogeneous p-tau217-positive population.

Strength of evidence

Moderate-to-strong clinical-validity evidence from six cohorts with amyloid PET and longitudinal outcomes. It remains observational, uses cohort- and assay-specific thresholds, does not establish incremental performance over full clinical models, and provides no prospective decision-impact or outcome evidence.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

Dual GFAP and p-tau217 measurement may help enrich trials or identify research participants at greater progression risk, but this paper does not support a universal clinical cutoff or prove that management changes based on the combination improve outcomes.

Field medical relevance

Relevant to prognostic claims, trial enrichment and interpretation of a positive p-tau217 result. It separates added prognostic association from analytical validation, authorization and clinical utility.

Quanterix or platform relevance

GFAP and p-tau217 positivity was defined within cohort and assay rather than with a single clinically validated cross-platform threshold. The prognostic association therefore does not establish interchangeable cut points or transferability to a specific commercial assay.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No assay authorization, availability, guideline endorsement, coverage or reimbursement change follows from this report.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Does GFAP diagnose Alzheimer disease?
No. GFAP reflects astrocyte reactivity and is not specific to Alzheimer disease; this analysis used it to stratify progression among groups defined with p-tau217 and amyloid PET.
Can one commercial cutoff be used from this study?
No. Assays and positivity definitions were cohort-specific, so the study does not establish a single transferable clinical threshold.
Is clinical utility established?
No. The study did not test whether acting on combined GFAP and p-tau217 results changes treatment decisions, counseling quality or patient outcomes.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Observational pooled analysis cannot establish that astrocyte reactivity causes faster decline
  • Cohort-specific assays and positivity thresholds limit direct cross-platform implementation
  • GFAP is biologically nonspecific and may reflect non-Alzheimer processes
  • The worsening hazard estimate was modest and its 95% confidence interval began at 1.01
  • No analytical-validation, prospective decision-impact or clinical-utility study

Primary source · DOI · Open-access full article

Bellaver B, Povala G, Ferreira PCL, et al; HEAD study. Astrocyte reactivity identifies p-tau217-positive individuals at elevated risk of cognitive decline across the Alzheimer's disease continuum. Mol Neurodegener. Published online September 21, 2026. doi:10.1186/s13024-026-00995-5.

Practice-relevant•Peer-reviewed randomized clinical trial and prespecified delayed-access follow-up•September 21, 2026

WeCareAdvisor yields modest caregiver benefits, not fewer behaviors

In 262 dementia caregivers, immediate WeCareAdvisor access did not significantly improve any of three prespecified outcomes at the three-month timepoint, but longitudinal distress and secondary wellbeing measures favored immediate use; delayed access produced fewer gains and one fewer DICE session.

Key quantitative results: At three months, none of the three prespecified timepoint comparisons was significant: behavior frequency-by-severity p=0.14, caregiver distress p=0.074 and confidence p=0.19. The longitudinal distress interaction was significant (Bonferroni-corrected p=0.012); post hoc distress fell 5.3 points with immediate versus 2.1 with delayed access, difference-in-differences 3.3 (95% CI 1.1 to 5.4; p=0.0031; Cohen d=0.386).

Clinical TrialsManagementCaregiver support

Added September 22, 2026 · NCT05012410; DOI:10.1093/geront/gnag226; PMID:42767991; supporting DOI:10.1111/jgs.70637

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

WeCareAdvisor operationalizes the DICE approach in a web app that tailors non-drug strategies to behavioral symptoms and possible triggers. The trial supports modest caregiver-distress and wellbeing gains, not a clear reduction in patient behaviors, and the new follow-up suggests that providing access earlier may improve engagement and the breadth of benefit.

Study design

A nationwide trial randomized 262 community-living caregivers of people with dementia to immediate access (n=131) or three-month delayed access (n=131). Masked interviewers assessed three primary outcomes and seven prespecified secondary outcomes through three months; the September 21 report compared engagement and outcomes after delayed users received access during months three to six.

Key quantitative results

  • At three months, none of the three prespecified timepoint comparisons was significant: behavior frequency-by-severity p=0.14, caregiver distress p=0.074 and confidence p=0.19. The longitudinal distress interaction was significant (Bonferroni-corrected p=0.012); post hoc distress fell 5.3 points with immediate versus 2.1 with delayed access, difference-in-differences 3.3 (95% CI 1.1 to 5.4; p=0.0031; Cohen d=0.386).
  • Caregiver wellbeing improved in 52% of immediate users versus 27% of delayed controls at three months (p=0.0003). Secondary outcomes also favored immediate use for wellbeing and upset with functional decline, but multiplicity was not controlled for these exploratory comparisons.
  • In the new delayed-access analysis, delayed users completed 3.1 DICE sessions versus 4.2 among immediate users (p=0.0052). Delayed users improved in wellbeing (p<0.001) and confidence (p=0.0069) but not behavioral symptoms (p>0.05), and immediate users improved more on most outcomes.

What changed

A peer-reviewed delayed-access analysis now completes the randomized trial's six-month comparison and shows that later access was associated with less engagement and fewer areas of improvement, while confirming no clear change in behavioral symptoms.

Strength of evidence

Randomized prospective evidence with masked interviewers and low three-month attrition, but the trial used a waitlist rather than active control, did not meet its three prespecified timepoint outcomes, relied on caregiver report and was demographically narrow. Secondary and post hoc findings require cautious interpretation.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

The app may be a scalable adjunct for caregiver problem-solving and wellbeing, particularly when offered promptly, but it should not be presented as proven to reduce dementia-related behaviors or replace individualized clinical assessment of new or severe symptoms.

Field medical relevance

Directly relevant to supportive care, nonpharmacologic management and caregiver intervention discussions, including how timing and engagement affect real-world digital-tool benefit.

Access or reimbursement relevance

The publications establish no authorization, formal guideline endorsement, coverage or reimbursement policy. Public availability and implementation support for the app were not established by the trial reports.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Did the trial meet its primary outcomes?
Not at the prespecified three-month timepoint. The significant distress finding came from the longitudinal interaction, and the 3.3-point change contrast was a post hoc analysis.
Did the app reduce behavioral symptoms?
No clear timepoint benefit was shown for behavior frequency-by-severity, and delayed users also had no significant behavioral-symptom change after access.
Who was studied?
Community caregivers of people with dementia of varied etiologies; 67.9% were reported as Alzheimer disease and 32.1% as FTD, PPA or PSP. Most caregivers were female, White, highly educated and living with the person with dementia.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • No significant immediate-versus-delayed difference for any of the three prespecified primary outcomes at the three-month timepoint
  • Waitlist control without an attention-matched digital comparator
  • Caregiver-reported outcomes and no blinded participant exposure
  • Predominantly White, female and college-educated caregiver sample with internet access
  • Mixed dementia etiologies and exploratory secondary analyses without multiplicity adjustment

Primary source · DOI · Primary three-month randomized trial report · ClinicalTrials.gov record · PubMed record

Gitlin LN, McClure LA, Webster MJ, Lyketsos C, Kales HC. Timing Matters: Effects of Delayed versus Immediate Access to a Web-Based Application on Caregiver Outcomes: The WeCareAdvisor Trial. Gerontologist. Published online September 21, 2026. doi:10.1093/geront/gnag226.

Important new evidence•Peer-reviewed retrospective longitudinal cohort analysis•September 19, 2026

ADNI analysis separates GFAP signal from weak vascular markers

Across biomarker-specific ADNI samples, Simoa GFAP rose stepwise from cognitively unimpaired participants to MCI and Alzheimer disease and distinguished AD from unimpaired participants with AUC 0.822, while sTREM2 and the vascular markers showed substantial overlap and no individual-level diagnostic utility.

Key quantitative results: Baseline GFAP was 21.5% higher in MCI than cognitively unimpaired participants (95% CI 13.1%–30.6%) and 56.3% higher in AD (40.4%–74.2%; multiplicity-adjusted q=1.66×10⁻14). AD-versus-unimpaired discrimination was AUC 0.822 (95% CI 0.779–0.866), Cohen d=1.23, with distributional overlap of 0.51.

BiomarkersBloodGFAPsTREM2Disease characterization

Added September 20, 2026 · DOI:10.1096/fba.2026-00194; PMID:42763575; PMCID:PMC13589249

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

GFAP produced strong group-level separation, but this was a clinical-diagnosis analysis rather than an amyloid- or tau-defined diagnostic-validation study. sTREM2 was null at baseline, vascular-marker distributions overlapped heavily, and none of the measures was tested for clinical decision impact.

Study design

Secondary ADNI analysis of 2,650 covariate-complete participants: 1,027 cognitively unimpaired, 1,187 with mild cognitive impairment and 436 with Alzheimer disease. Baseline assay samples differed by platform: GFAP n=832, sTREM2 n=1,001 and vascular markers n=566. Longitudinal analyses included 1,252 participants and 1,671 GFAP observations, 1,031 participants and 1,771 sTREM2 observations, and 566 participants and 1,061 vascular-marker observations.

Key quantitative results

  • Baseline GFAP was 21.5% higher in MCI than cognitively unimpaired participants (95% CI 13.1%–30.6%) and 56.3% higher in AD (40.4%–74.2%; multiplicity-adjusted q=1.66×10⁻14). AD-versus-unimpaired discrimination was AUC 0.822 (95% CI 0.779–0.866), Cohen d=1.23, with distributional overlap of 0.51.
  • sTREM2 did not separate AD from unimpaired participants at baseline: +2.2% (95% CI −7.4% to 12.8%; q=0.769), AUC 0.507. VEGF and sVCAM-1 were modestly higher in AD, with AUCs of 0.612 and 0.625, while vascular-marker overlap was at least 0.83; sICAM-1 was not significant.
  • GFAP increased 4.50% per year in cognitively unimpaired participants (95% CI 3.79%–5.21%) and sTREM2 increased 2.99% per year (1.56%–4.44%), but diagnosis-by-time interactions were not significant after multiplicity correction. The vascular panel showed divergent 12-month patterns that require replication.

What changed

A single longitudinal ADNI analysis directly compared glial and vascular plasma markers across disease groups and quantified both group separation and longitudinal change on three assay platforms.

Strength of evidence

Moderate exploratory clinical-validity evidence from a large, well-characterized research cohort. Clinical groups were not defined against an amyloid or tau reference standard, assay availability was nonrandom and most GFAP and sTREM2 participants had only one measurement. The study provides no analytical-validation or clinical-utility evidence.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

The findings support plasma GFAP as a research marker of glial activation with meaningful group-level separation, not as a stand-alone AD diagnostic or stage marker. The sTREM2 and vascular-marker findings do not support individual-level interpretation.

Field medical relevance

The study helps MSL teams distinguish a reproducible GFAP research signal from weaker exploratory vascular-marker findings and clarifies why diagnostic separation, assay validity and clinical utility should not be conflated.

Quanterix or platform relevance

The signals are assay- and dataset-specific. The study did not establish transferability across GFAP, sTREM2 or vascular-marker platforms, laboratories or cut points.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No assay authorization, commercial-availability, guideline-endorsement, coverage or reimbursement change follows from this analysis.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Was Alzheimer disease confirmed with amyloid or tau biomarkers?
No. The primary comparisons used clinical diagnosis groups, so the study does not establish AD-specific validity against a biological reference standard.
Did the study validate the assays analytically?
No. It analyzed existing platform-specific ADNI data and did not establish precision, interference, cross-platform equivalence or clinical cut points.
Can these markers be used for clinical decisions?
Not from this study. It did not test decision impact, patient outcomes, implementation thresholds or clinical utility.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Clinical diagnosis groups rather than an amyloid- or tau-defined reference standard
  • Retrospective secondary analysis with nonrandom and platform-specific assay availability
  • Most GFAP and sTREM2 participants contributed only one measurement
  • Vascular-marker follow-up was limited to 12 months and glial-vascular correlations used only 64 to 94 overlapping participants
  • No analytical validation, prospective decision-impact study or clinical-utility assessment

Primary source · DOI · PubMed Central full text · PubMed record

Jahanbin K; Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative. Glial and Vascular Plasma Biomarkers Across the Alzheimer's Disease Continuum: An ADNI-Based Longitudinal Study. FASEB BioAdvances. Published online September 19, 2026. doi:10.1096/fba.2026-00194.

The second edition expands prevention guidance, including environmental exposure and tailored multidomain interventions.

Key recommendations: Recommendations include physical activity, cardiometabolic care, social engagement, and reducing air-pollution exposure.

GuidelinesManagementRisk reduction

Added September 7, 2026 · WHO ISBN 978-92-4-012355-7

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

This is guidance for normal cognition and MCI, not evidence that established AD dementia can be reversed.

Evidence basis and population

WHO evidence synthesis for adults without dementia, with a life-course and public-health focus.

Key recommendations

Updates the 2019 edition.

Does the 45% estimate describe an individual treatment effect?

CELIA misses its primary dose-response endpoint despite encouraging secondary signals

Sponsor-reported phase 2 findings support further study of diranersen; they do not establish treatment benefit.

Key quantitative results: At 60 mg every 6 months (n=60) versus placebo (n=115), the reported CDR-SB difference was −0.54 points, or 26% less decline. Confidence intervals were not supplied in the cited release.

Clinical TrialsManagementCSFTotal tauTau PETDisease-modifying treatment

Added September 7, 2026 · NCT05399888

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The primary endpoint failed, and favorable secondary comparisons require confirmation.

Study design

CELIA randomized 416 anti-amyloid-naive participants with MCI or mild AD dementia to intrathecal diranersen or placebo for 18 months.

Key quantitative results

  • At 60 mg every 6 months (n=60) versus placebo (n=115), the reported CDR-SB difference was −0.54 points, or 26% less decline. Confidence intervals were not supplied in the cited release.
  • The 115 mg regimens showed smaller CDR-SB differences (−0.28 and −0.18); ADCS-ADL-MCI did not separate from placebo.

What changed

July data quantify the earlier topline announcement.

Strength of evidence

Randomized design, but conference/sponsor reporting with a failed primary endpoint.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

Insufficient for clinical use.

Field medical relevance

Keep nominal secondary findings separate from confirmatory evidence.

Quanterix or platform relevance

Tau reduction does not establish an assay’s clinical utility.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No approval, availability or coverage claim.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Was the study positive on its primary endpoint?
No. Dose response on CDR-SB was not demonstrated.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Multiplicity, small lowest-dose group, and absent confidence intervals.
  • Full independent peer-reviewed assessment was not verified.

Lecanemab labeling adds subcutaneous treatment initiation

The July label permits weekly subcutaneous initiation, extending home-injection options beyond maintenance treatment.

Key label details: Subcutaneous starting dose is 500 mg weekly, as two 250 mg injections. After 18 months, continuing that regimen or transitioning to maintenance is permitted.

ManagementDisease-modifying treatment

Added September 7, 2026 · BLA 761375/S-001; FDA label reference 5833017

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

Route convenience changes delivery planning, while amyloid confirmation, early symptomatic eligibility and ARIA precautions remain.

Study design

Label update for initiation in MCI or mild AD dementia, with confirmed amyloid pathology.

Key label details

  • Subcutaneous starting dose is 500 mg weekly, as two 250 mg injections. After 18 months, continuing that regimen or transitioning to maintenance is permitted.
  • Subcutaneous maintenance is 360 mg weekly. The label specifies baseline MRI and monitoring after 1, 2, 3 and 6 months.

What changed

Subcutaneous dosing can begin at treatment initiation.

Strength of evidence

Authoritative dosing instructions; not a new head-to-head clinical-benefit trial.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

Initiation and maintenance strengths must remain distinct.

Field medical relevance

Discuss delivery burden together with safety infrastructure.

Access or reimbursement relevance

FDA authorization is verified. Current supply, coverage and patient cost are not established here.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Does home dosing remove ARIA monitoring?
No. The boxed warning and MRI surveillance still apply.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • This route change does not establish superior cognition outcomes or lower ARIA risk.
